title: Further Scaling Our Malaria Grantmaking
content:
Over the past five years, GiveWell has expanded the scale of our grantmaking and team substantially. We expect to grant more than $1 billion this year, more than double the $418 million we committed in 2025. Alongside this grantmaking growth, we’ve more than doubled the number of researchers on our team since the start of last year. A larger team means we can investigate a greater number of both more complex and larger funding opportunities than we could before. One area where we expect our grantmaking to increase substantially in the coming years is the prevention and treatment of malaria.

From 2027 through 2032, we’re aiming to grant at least $2.5 billion in new malaria funding, potentially several times that amount. The total amount will depend on the funding we have available, the feasibility of scaling up cost-effective malaria programs, countries’ appetite for those programs, and how opportunities within malaria compare to other grantmaking areas. This expanded support could go to organizations we currently fund (such as the Against Malaria Foundation and Malaria Consortium), as well as to new organizations and novel funding vehicles. We are still in the process of assessing which strategies for deploying new malaria funding are likely to be highly cost-effective and scalable, and are currently exploring partnerships with the Global Fund and Gavi to help rapidly scale our impact across many programs in many countries at once.

While this post focuses on our malaria work, we are also growing our grantmaking in other areas. This includes areas we have supported for many years, such as treatment for severe malnutrition, efforts to increase childhood vaccination, and programs to provide safe drinking water, as well as areas we have supported at relatively smaller scale to date, such as medical oxygen, tuberculosis control, and family planning. We currently expect to grant more than $1 billion to program areas outside malaria in 2027, and we think we could grant more with additional funding. While the scale of our grantmaking is growing, we’ll remain focused on researching the most cost‑effective ways to save and improve lives, sharing our work openly, and directing donations to help people in need as much as we can.

*   [Why malaria?](http://blog.givewell.org/2026/10/26/further-scaling-our-malaria-grantmaking#Why_malaria)
*   [What and how much might we fund?](http://blog.givewell.org/2026/10/26/further-scaling-our-malaria-grantmaking#What_and_how_much)
*   [How long will we fund programs?](http://blog.givewell.org/2026/10/26/further-scaling-our-malaria-grantmaking#How_long)
*   [The Malaria Impact Accelerator partnership with the Global Fund](http://blog.givewell.org/2026/10/26/further-scaling-our-malaria-grantmaking#Accelerator)
    *   [Why the Global Fund?](http://blog.givewell.org/2026/10/26/further-scaling-our-malaria-grantmaking#Global_Fund)

*   [Building the data to scale well](http://blog.givewell.org/2026/10/26/further-scaling-our-malaria-grantmaking#Data)
    *   [Where should funding be targeted, and for which programs?](http://blog.givewell.org/2026/10/26/further-scaling-our-malaria-grantmaking#Target)
    *   [What opportunities are there to improve the quality of implementation?](http://blog.givewell.org/2026/10/26/further-scaling-our-malaria-grantmaking#Implementation)
    *   [How can we estimate the impact of our funding?](http://blog.givewell.org/2026/10/26/further-scaling-our-malaria-grantmaking#Impact)

*   [What we’re working on and what comes next](http://blog.givewell.org/2026/10/26/further-scaling-our-malaria-grantmaking#Next)

## Why malaria?

Malaria kills around 600,000 people each year, most of whom are young children.[[1]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#1) We know how to prevent, diagnose, and treat malaria. Effective prevention can be provided via vector control (especially [long-lasting insecticide-treated nets](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion-technical-notes#ITNs)), [chemoprevention](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion-technical-notes#SMC), and [vaccination](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion-technical-notes#malaria_vaccines).[[2]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#2) Inexpensive rapid diagnostic tests can be used to identify when people have been infected with malaria,[[3]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#3) and artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) or injectable artesunate are highly effective treatments.[[4]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#4) However, many people in countries where malaria is endemic do not have access to prevention and treatment.[[5]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#5)

Governments of malaria-endemic countries fund a substantial part of their own malaria responses,[[6]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#6) but in many high-burden countries, domestic budgets alone cannot cover what is needed. In addition, recent declines in health aid have widened gaps that already existed. Donors pledged $12.6 billion for the Global Fund’s latest replenishment, down from $15.7 billion three years earlier and well short of the $18 billion target.[[7]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#7) As a result, the Global Fund has allocated $3.5 billion to countries for its next three years of malaria grants, about 15% less than in the previous three-year cycle.[[8]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#8) Gavi, which funds malaria vaccines, raised just under $10 billion of its $11.9 billion budget for 2026–2030 and reduced the malaria vaccine coverage it will fund as a result.[[9]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#9) At the same time, newer tools that could drive significant advances, such as dual-ingredient nets designed to counter insecticide resistance, cost more than older ones.[[10]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#10)

Malaria control has long been a central focus of our work. In total, GiveWell has directed more than $1.3 billion to malaria prevention and treatment, including more than $750 million for nets and more than $500 million for seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC), which we estimate will save more than [300,000 lives](https://blog.givewell.org/2026/05/28/growing-givewells-largest-research-area-malaria/).

[![Image 1: Bar chart with gray and blue bars](https://blog.givewell.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Malaria-funding-chart.png)](https://blog.givewell.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Malaria-funding-chart.png)

Malaria stands out among the areas we’re exploring for expanded grantmaking because such large funding gaps exist for programs that have strong evidence of effectiveness and that GiveWell has experience funding. This contrasts with other grantmaking areas we’re exploring, where we’re earlier in our understanding. We expect to make more grants and larger grants in some of these other areas as we learn more about them.

## What and how much might we fund?

To identify programs[[11]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#11) we might fund through our expanded malaria portfolio, we looked for those that have evidence of reducing illness and death, are feasible to deliver where malaria is most common, and could fit with national priorities. We’ve also focused our analysis to date on programs where we expect the largest funding gaps to exist, since those areas could make the biggest difference to how much funding we allocate.

Based on this initial work, we see room for at least $2.5 billion in grantmaking to malaria programs from 2027 through 2032 at our current cost-effectiveness bar (you can read more about [the role of cost-effectiveness in our funding decisions](https://blog.givewell.org/2023/10/27/how-we-work-1-cost-effectiveness/)). With more funding, we could grant substantially more, potentially at a lower cost-effectiveness bar.

Our early expectation is that most of this funding could go to support the programs below. The list focuses on programs that could be both cost-effective and have large funding gaps.[[12]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#12)

Note, however, that this list is neither comprehensive nor final. We expect to update the list of potential programs over time and to update our view of the programs listed as we do more research and learn from national malaria programs and other implementers.

*   Prevention programs, such as [insecticide-treated nets](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion-technical-notes#ITNs), [seasonal malaria chemoprevention](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion-technical-notes#SMC) (SMC), and [malaria vaccines](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion-technical-notes#malaria_vaccines), including running these programs more often or reaching people these programs do not currently cover.
*   Testing and treatment programs and commodities, such as case management by [community health workers](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion-technical-notes#iCCM), and [support for supply chains](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion-technical-notes#supply_chain) that transport diagnostic tests and treatment drugs to clinics. 
*   [Newer tools](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion-technical-notes#newer_tools), such as [spatial emanators](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion-technical-notes#spatial_emanators) and insecticide-treated babywraps, provided they are supported by sufficient high-quality evidence. We expect to fund some of that evidence generation ourselves, including additional randomized trials. 

[The technical notes](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion-technical-notes) for each program summarize our current understanding and uncertainties. Overall, we’re more confident in our understanding of net campaigns and SMC for young children, which we’ve funded at a large scale for years now. We’re still developing our understanding of the cost-effectiveness of approaches like supporting community health workers and support for supply chains, chemoprevention for older children, and efforts to increase coverage of the malaria vaccine and newer tools at scale.

The most cost-effective mix of programs will also vary from place to place. For example, a given program may be highly cost-effective where malaria is common, the program is feasible to implement, and few people have alternative sources of malaria prevention, and much less so where the reverse is true.

Alongside multiyear grants for these programs, we expect to fund supporting work such as monitoring and evaluation, evidence generation, operational research, market shaping, technical assistance, advocacy, and possibly research and development.

GiveWell uses a cost-effectiveness threshold that helps us decide whether to provide funding to a program. We currently fund programs that are at least 6 times more cost-effective than [our benchmark](https://www.givewell.org/how-we-work/our-criteria/cost-effectiveness/cost-effectiveness-models). We have rough projections of how much malaria funding we could grant at different levels of cost-effectiveness, but these are early estimates that we expect to change substantially as we do more research and learn from national programs and implementers about which programs they want to prioritize and can deliver well. In the future, the threshold we use to make funding decisions may change depending on how much funding we raise and what outcomes we believe can be achieved.

## How long will we fund programs?

We’re working to secure the resources needed to support these programs for five to six years. We think this will let us fund more cost-effective programs more quickly. Expanding a malaria program takes upfront work, like planning, hiring and training staff, and setting up operations in new locations. In our experience, national programs and other implementers are more willing to take that on if they expect funding to last long enough for the work to pay off. With only a short funding period, many would reasonably expand less, leading to less impact.

A longer time frame also means we can act on the evidence we help build. We expect to fund studies of some newer tools. If evidence shows a tool works and can be delivered well, we want to have funding ready to deliver it at scale, ensuring the evidence translates quickly into impact.

Our intention is to renew the initial grants, which will likely cover about two to three years of programming, and we plan to set aside the funding to continue programming when we make initial commitments. Before renewing, we will consider whether governments are interested in continuing the programs and whether they’re having the expected outcomes (e.g., whether coverage surveys show they’re reaching the people they’re meant to, and whether malaria prevalence is falling in the areas they cover). Many of the programs we’re considering are ambitious and new at this scale, such as running net campaigns more often or extending chemoprevention to older children, and we, alongside national programs and other implementers, expect to learn a lot in the first few years about what works. We’ll also consider whether other funding for malaria programs has gone down, because we intend for our funding to add to what governments and other donors already spend, not replace it.

If we decide to reduce or end funding after an initial grant, we plan to give national governments and other implementers as much notice as we can and to step funding down gradually. As we do with our existing grantees, we expect to provide exit funding to allow for a well-managed wind-down. Where we can, we’ll also design programs so that governments or other funders can more easily continue them.

## The Malaria Impact Accelerator partnership with the Global Fund

The Malaria Impact Accelerator is a proposed partnership between GiveWell and the Global Fund, and one of several ways we are considering directing our expanded malaria funding. It would build on the Global Fund’s processes, with a few key differences.[[13]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#13) First, the funding through this partnership would be specific to malaria[[14]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#14) and allocations to countries through this partnership would be more proportionate to malaria burden than the Global Fund’s core allocations. As a result, in comparison to the Global Fund’s typical processes, we expect funds allocated through the Malaria Impact Accelerator will go to a smaller number of higher burden countries. Additionally, the funding would only support programs we assess to be above our cost-effectiveness bar. We would also fund independent monitoring of these programs and publish the results.

The proposed Malaria Impact Accelerator has three main components: (1) country “investment requests,” which are plans countries would submit for how they would use additional funds, (2) a “fast track” for urgent needs, and (3) funding for complementary work.

We expect most funding in the Malaria Impact Accelerator to support country “investment requests,” giving countries additional funds to support their national malaria priorities. GiveWell and the Global Fund would jointly set a maximum funding allocation for each eligible country and provide guidance on which programs are eligible and how cost-effectiveness will shape funding decisions. We would also fund technical support for countries that want it in preparing their requests. Each country, operating through existing Country Coordinating Mechanisms,[[15]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#15) would choose the programs it wants to include in its investment requests based on its own priorities, including those in its National Strategic Plans. Requests would be reviewed by the Global Fund’s existing Technical Review Panel for technical soundness and by GiveWell for cost-effectiveness, and countries would have an opportunity to revise requests in response to feedback before GiveWell and the Global Fund’s final joint funding decisions.[[16]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#16)

Because these requests take time to prepare and review, we also expect to run a “fast track” to fund urgent gaps countries have already identified as priorities in highly cost-effective programs.

Finally, we expect to set aside some funding for complementary work that doesn’t fit within a single country’s request. This funding could support bringing new tools to market, making tools more affordable, or generating evidence on questions that help us make better funding decisions.

##### Why the Global Fund

We think partnering with the Global Fund is the fastest way to scale up malaria funding, reduce malaria burden, and support national malaria responses. The Global Fund is the largest international funder of malaria programs, disbursing roughly $1 billion to $1.5 billion a year for malaria over the past decade.[[17]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#17) It has long-standing relationships and established funding processes in the countries where malaria burden and funding gaps are highest. Working within those processes means countries won’t need an entirely separate process to work with us. In addition, the Global Fund has financial controls and an independent audit office to help prevent fraud and waste.

We’ll decide how much to grant through the Malaria Impact Accelerator as we do more research on the funding opportunities, see applications from countries, and get more information from the Global Fund. However, there are a few considerations that could lead us to grant less than expected through this mechanism, or none at all:

*   **The Global Fund’s commitment and capacity.** The Global Fund’s board has yet to approve the mechanism. It will soon select a new executive director and seat its recently elected board leadership. The partnership depends on sustained commitment from Global Fund leadership and on the Global Fund executing well. We expect to contribute funding to the Secretariat’s operations, including dedicated staff capacity to support this, and we’ll be watching for continued engagement through the duration of the partnership. 
*   **Track record of Global Fund-funded programming.** We want to understand how many people Global Fund-supported programs reach and where coverage could be improved. To do this, we’re funding independent coverage surveys and qualitative research after recent campaigns, and triangulating with coverage surveys from other sources where possible. If coverage appears lower than we expect and difficult to improve, we may grant less funding through the mechanism. 
*   **What we learn from countries.** Once we tell a country its maximum funding amount, that funding will be available for requests that meet our cost-effectiveness bar. As countries plan and submit investment requests, we may find that interest in some programs we think are highly cost-effective is lower than we expected, or that they are harder to deliver at scale than we expect. This could lead GiveWell to grant less funding overall or similar amounts at a slower pace. 
*   **Longer-term risks.** Increased philanthropic funding could lead governments and other donors to cut their own malaria spending, or could strain health systems. We plan to engage with governments and donors to emphasize that our funding is intended to be additional to theirs, and that its impact depends on their continued vital investments. We’re exploring matched funding and advocacy to encourage them to sustain their spending. We also expect to fund health systems investments that support malaria programs, and to monitor whether other care is affected. If we think there is likely to be substantial risk of crowding out or negative spillovers to the broader health system that we are unable to mitigate, it could cause us to grant less funding. 

In the event we direct less funding than expected or no funding through this partnership with the Global Fund, we would plan to scale up malaria funding through other grantees, including organizations we fund today.

## Building the data to scale well

We plan to fund additional data collection, monitoring, and strengthening of existing data systems so that national malaria programs, other implementers, and funders, including GiveWell, have better information for their decisions. We think these efforts could help answer key questions for both malaria and non-malaria programs:

1.   Where should funding be targeted and for which programs? 
2.   What opportunities are there to improve the quality of implementation? 
3.   How can GiveWell estimate the impact of our funding? 

##### Where should funding be targeted, and for which programs?

Decisions about where to direct resources for malaria programming mostly rely on routine health facility data, which can be inaccurate in areas with a high malaria burden,[[18]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#18) and on national household surveys that run every few years at best.[[19]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#19)

With national malaria programs’ agreement and collaboration, we plan to fund nationally representative household surveys in countries where we may grant substantial additional funding, to be completed prior to our key funding decisions, and to strengthen the routine data that national programs collect from health facilities and hospitals. Together, these should give better estimates of malaria prevalence, severe malaria, child mortality, and program coverage. Some of the same data will also be useful for other programs. For example, the household surveys will ask whether children received vitamin A supplements in the past six months. This could give health ministries additional information on where supplementation is hitting coverage targets and where more support might be needed. We also expect to fund monitoring of drug and insecticide resistance and of mosquito populations. Current monitoring has significant geographic gaps, and resistance can make programs less effective over time.[[20]](https://www.givewell.org/sources/blog-post/malaria-expansion#20)

Better data would help in tailoring programs to local conditions, identifying emerging risks to program efficacy, and directing newer tools to the areas that need them.

##### What opportunities are there to improve the quality of implementation?

Many health programs report the number of people reached from implementers’ own records, which raises concerns about data completeness, data quality, and the potential for bias. We expect to fund independent household coverage surveys, which estimate what share of the eligible population was reached, and visits to a sample of people recorded as receiving services to check that they did.

We think that funding to strengthen existing data collection systems can help implementers identify and fix implementation issues while programs are running. For example, an unexpected increase in malaria among pregnant women at their first antenatal visit could signal that prevention efforts in that area aren’t reaching people or working as intended. Signs of growing drug or insecticide resistance could prompt a switch to a different drug or type of net. Finally, we will explore support to other modes of learning about program implementation such as community-led monitoring.

##### How can we estimate the impact of our funding?

Most estimates of the impact of large health programs, including GiveWell’s, are modeled or extrapolated using data from administrative systems, infrequent surveys, and/or older trials run in different settings and at smaller scale. We’re considering two approaches that may allow us to more directly measure the impact of increased malaria funding on prevalence and mortality.

*   We could compare changes in prevalence and mortality between areas that receive more of our funding and areas that receive less, and treat the difference as the effect of our funding. This gives a causal estimate if the two sets of areas would have changed in the same way without our funding. To make it more likely this assumption holds, we would likely restrict the comparison to the most similar areas. 
*   We could use the way individual programs are rolled out to compare similar groups that do and do not receive the program. For example, chemoprevention programs typically target only certain ages, so we could compare children just above and below that limit to estimate program impact. These comparisons are more credibly causal, but each one covers only a small part of what we fund and misses how programs work in combination. 

We will adapt our approach to data collection over time as we further define our scaling plans and learn more from governments and other implementers. Some specific uncertainties include:

*   **Specific support for national malaria control programs and implementers.** We’re eager to learn from national malaria programs and implementers about how best to ensure that these efforts can be used to help with planning and program improvements. We know that one strategy is to share results using systems and formats they already use. Over the next few months, we expect to share results from data collection we’re already funding and will work to learn more about the best ways to support governments and implementers in using these data and to strengthen existing data systems. 
*   **Timing.** It’s possible that some of the surveys we plan to fund may not generate findings prior to the funding decisions we intend them to inform. While this would reduce their usefulness for that purpose, the data could potentially be used to inform governments and other implementers. In addition, if we think surveys could not be completed in time to inform particular decisions, we may choose to spend less on them. 
*   **Attribution of impact.** We may not be able to attribute changes in malaria or mortality to our funding. Doing so depends on comparable regions receiving funding at different times or intensities, which we may not control. We are also likely to be underpowered to detect effects on mortality for several years. 
*   **Sustainability of these data systems.** Countries may not want or be able to keep paying for these data if our funding ends. We’re exploring ways to test cheaper methods that would be easier to sustain without external support (such as phone surveys, data gathered during routine health facility visits, and prediction models) against more expensive data collection techniques, such as in-person household surveys. 

## What we’re working on and what comes next

As with the rest of our grantmaking, we expect our malaria plans to evolve as we learn from new research, from conversations with governments and other partners, and from new data collected from the programs we fund. To drive this work forward, in the coming months we expect to:

*   **Update our understanding of the cost-effectiveness of programs and real-world funding gaps.** By reviewing published research and having conversations with experts at all levels, national malaria programs, and our partners, we’re working to deepen our understanding of the impact and cost-effectiveness of specific programs we could fund. We are also working to better understand which programs are already funded and where gaps remain in the countries where we expect to fund the most. 
*   **Fund immediate gaps that we know about.** Some countries have already planned highly cost-effective programs, such as net campaigns, that they can’t pay for. We expect to support these programs in whichever way makes the most sense. This may mean approving grants to the Against Malaria Foundation or Malaria Consortium, two of our current grantees; funding the programs through the Malaria Impact Accelerator’s fast track; or potentially funding other implementing organizations. 
*   **Fund baseline data collection.** With national programs’ approval, we expect to fund household surveys in countries where we may end up directing the most funding. These would measure malaria prevalence, child mortality, and program coverage before funding scales up. We’re also finishing the review of coverage surveys of recent Global Fund-supported campaigns described above. 
*   **Take the next steps on new partnerships.** If the Global Fund’s board approves the Malaria Impact Accelerator mechanism and we decide to move forward with the partnership, we expect to work with Global Fund staff to set country allocations, publish the guidance described above, and begin funding technical support for countries that want it. At the same time, we’re exploring partnerships with other organizations, including funding malaria vaccines through Gavi, which could help us reach more people with cost-effective malaria programs. 

We’ll keep updating our plans as this work progresses, and we plan to share what we learn along the way.

title: The half-life of disappointment
content:
When things don’t turn out the way you pictured, how long does it take for you to move on?

Reducing this window of disappointment unlocks the path to creativity and leadership.

People who get over disappointment more quickly aren’t less excited about the project than the others. They realize that getting attached to an outcome doesn’t increase its likelihood, and in fact, makes it less likely that their next project will be as bold.

Turns out that this is a common practice among professionals in every field.

title: When Texas Bat “Cities” Look Like Thunderstorms
content:
For at least 8,500 years, the community inside Texas’ Bracken Cave has swelled exponentially every spring as up to 10 million free-tailed bats fly 700 miles north from various smaller roosts in and around central Mexico. After mother bats give birth to their pups, the population will double again to [nearly 20 million](https://www.tpr.org/arts-culture/2024-07-16/batnado-at-bracken-cave-is-an-incredible-natural-phenomenon-with-twenty-million-players)—the largest congregation of nonhuman mammals on Earth.

By midsummer, the millions of hungry pups grow restless as food demand reaches its zenith. The result is a nightly commute of epic proportions, as legions of nocturnal hunters, young and old, flood into the surrounding fields—an event known simply as “the emergence.”

At its peak, Bracken’s population is so dense that it takes over three and a half hours for every bat to hurtle out of the cave’s bottleneck entrance, creating a plume of tiny flapping wings that resembles a serpent extending into the evening sky. Soaring up to 10,000 feet, the adults and pups fan outward, traveling between 60 and 100 miles a night and collectively consuming more than 150 tons of moths, beetles, and other insects, before returning to their hideaway home just before daybreak.

As I watched this mesmerizing scene play out in person from the rim of the cave, one of the cave docents held up his phone to show me the live Doppler radar feed. The nearby New Braunfels radar station, which continuously scans the horizon for approaching thunderheads, soon picked up a massive blob larger than metropolitan San Antonio.

Weather apps generally modify their default settings to remove such scenes from view, the docent said. Otherwise, even on a clear night, people watching the radar feed would break out their umbrellas, believing they were about to get caught in a torrential downpour.

Bat emergences resemble thunderstorms on Doppler radar. _Credit: Austin Bat Refuge_

**Detecting Animal Metropolises Within Humanity’s Urban Sprawl**

There is no universal criteria for what defines a “city” beyond the [dictionary definition](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/city) of an inhabited place of comparatively greater size, population, or importance than a town or village. Generally speaking, it’s understood to be an area in which a large number of individuals gather or live in close physical proximity, usually to gain certain community advantages. In practice, cities also often serve as centralized hubs where cultural activities are carried out. (In the United Kingdom, for instance, a city’s status was [once](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_status_in_the_United_Kingdom) tied to whether or not it had a cathedral.) It’s where the action happens. A space bound by a collective spirit that gives a city its beating heart.

Animal cities are not measured by their concrete, glass, or steel, but by the community itself and the tangible advantages that large-scale cohabitation provides. Safety in numbers, knowledge sharing, services and trade, and environmental changes tied to a population’s sizable footprint are just a few possible reasons for coming together en masse rather than going it alone.

As a general rule, the larger an animal community is, the more information is being passed around, and the better its residents can collectively sense the nuances of the landscape. The increased swirling of knowledge around a community can, in turn, contribute to a sort of collective intelligence.

Some fruit bats, for instance, maintain a mental map of all the trees that could potentially produce fruit, but they don’t always know which ones will bloom next. The speculative knowledge they gather while sussing out the local options is then shared by scent with their close contacts as part of tightly-knit social groups. We don’t know how tight-lipped or active the Bracken bats are about sharing their learnings, but Gary McCracken, a field biologist at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, who has conducted genetic analyses of the cave’s bats to make sense of their complex relationship dynamics, says “there’s definitely eavesdropping going on.”

When I recounted the staggering experience of watching an entire city of bats collectively burst into the open air to Lee Mackenzie and Dianne Odegard, co-founders of [Austin Bat Refuge](https://austinbatrefuge.org/), Dianne smiled and said, “Well, I don’t know if you’re familiar with Lee’s research that he’s been doing for eleven or twelve years. He’s done Doppler radar research every single day for over a decade monitoring the emergences,” she said. “He has ninety different points that he gets from Doppler radar data. He probably has more [data about bat emergences](https://austinbatrefuge.org/radar-3/) in Central Texas than anybody on Earth. I’m sure Lee would love to show you what he’s got.”

Lee grinned ear to ear. “Come with me.”

**An Opaque Megalopolis**

Seated in his home office, Lee explained that several years back he had registered for a special training course offered at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s National Severe Storms Laboratory in Norman, Oklahoma. The course was designed for US Air Force pilots and other military professionals who need to monitor Doppler weather information in real time. But Lee wanted to take things one step further.

Using raw data from weather stations in San Angelo, Granger, New Braunfels, and Brackettville—the four corners of what he refers to as the “Significant Bat Area of Central Texas”—NOAA agreed to build Lee a calculus-based algorithm that can translate the on-screen blobs into an estimate of how many individuals are in the air. “It’s crazy complicated,” he said.

As he showed me the previous night’s download, he zoomed out beyond Austin’s city limits to point to dozens of other emergences. “That’s Bracken there. That’s Frio Bat Cave. That’s a new place I’m trying to find out,” he said, lingering over an emergence in an area far away from any human roads.

“An unexplored cave, you think?” I asked.

“Probably. Nobody else knows about it because nobody’s looking—except us!”

The sources were carefully labeled based on Lee’s sleuthing. “Chiroptorium,” “Old Tunnel,” “Randolph Air Force Base”—the list went on and on. Highway overpasses, rural caves, construction sites. Bats make themselves at home in any place that fits their needs and desires, he said. And night after night, for more than a decade, he had downloaded massive data sets driven solely by his own curiosity.

A first-of-its-kind map based on Doppler data of bat emergences was created by renowned cartographer Oliver Uberti.

As Lee zoomed back out to the full view and paused, we sat in silent awe, reflecting on all that the radar revealed. As impressive as Bracken is, with its 100 tons of bats screeching nightly through a narrow cave mouth, even that overwhelming sight does not capture the true scale of what’s going on.

There are cities within cities. A seemingly infinite blur of Texas Hill Country landmarks, transit networks, and subcommunities that we are only just beginning to understand. An opaque megalopolis of epic proportions, cloaked in the shadow of nightfall. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Take a Look at the Country’s Newest National Park
content:
It may take a while to become as famous as Yosemite, the Grand Canyon, or Monument Valley, but the 12,000-acre Chiricahua area in southeast Arizona just became the 64th national park in the U.S.

Known as “the wonderland of rocks,” Chiricahua was shaped by ancient volcanic forces and contains a wealth of dramatic geological features. It also boasts a rich human history, including tales of the Chiricahua Apache who lived here long before colonization from the Spanish, the African-American soldiers who were stationed here in the 1880s, and homesteading families who moved here from the eastern U.S. in the late 1800s.

One highlight: [Massai Point](https://www.nps.gov/chir/learn/historyculture/massai-point.htm). Named after a Chiricahua Apache man born in the Mescal Mountains, the landmark features spires and columns carved into rhyolite rock (originally flowing lava) by millions of years of erosion.

A view from Massai Point. _Credit: NPS Photo/Katy Hooper_

With an act of Congress signed by President Donald J. Trump, the region got an upgrade from “National Monument,” which was its status for more than a century.

“While its name is changing, our commitment remains the same: Protecting this remarkable landscape and its cultural heritage while providing opportunities for visitors to experience and enjoy it for generations to come,” Jessica Bowron, Comptroller Exercising the Delegated Authority of the Director of the National Park Service, said in a [statement](https://www.nps.gov/chir/learn/news/chiricahua-national-monument-becomes-america-s-newest-national-park.htm).

Big Balanced Rock, one of the formations in the Heart of Rocks Loop. _Credit: NPS/C. Bubar_

Chiricahua’s change in status should mean more visitors and increased spending per visitor (people tend to [stay overnight more](https://headwaterseconomics.org/public-lands/protected-lands/national-monuments-redesignated-national-parks/) often at parks versus monuments).

And there’s lots to do at Chiricahua. By day, visitors can wander hiking trails or take scenic drives, spotting wildlife like Coues white-tailed deer, mountain lions, and Chiricahua and Apache fox squirrels. By night, there’s the opportunity to camp out in the wilderness and indulge in some stargazing.

Faraway Ranch was one of the first homesteads set up in the park. _Credit: NPS Photo_

The new national park, now the fourth in Arizona, is what’s known [as a sky island](https://www.nps.gov/chir/learn/nature/sky-islands.htm)—that is, an “island” of mountain and rock rising up from the “sea” of the desert. The island as a whole sits around 6,000 feet above the Sulphur Springs Valley, though the highest point is actually outside the park: The top of Chiricahua Peak is 9,795 feet above sea level.

Of course, there’s also a conservation aspect to achieving national park status. It’s written in [the original Organic Act of 1916](https://www.nps.gov/aboutus/index.htm) that one of the purposes of the parks system is “to conserve the scenery and the natural and historic objects and the wild life therein.”

Some 154 years after Yellowstone became the first national park, the number of recognized areas has now swelled to 64—but happily much of the fundamental mission remains the same. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Spike-Thumbed Dino Discovered in the United Kingdom
content:
When a new dinosaur species is announced, we all probably share a similar image of how it was discovered: a team of sweaty paleontologists, meticulously removing layers of dirt to uncover a skeleton. While that kind of fieldwork still happens, plenty of dinosaurs are “discovered” in museum collections. Instead of waiting to be unearthed, these already excavated specimens have been waiting for the right PhD candidate to come along, agonizingly study them, and then document the details.

The latest species of dinosaur—an iguanodon relative described for the first time in a [study](http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/14772019.2026.2726221) published today—took the latter path, but with a twist. The specimen was discovered in the site of the Ewhurst brick and roof tile works, a clay quarry in Surrey, England, and the researchers recognized the team that did some actual digging. The species name, _Paludohadros proudlovii_, honors Will Proudlove, a beloved former manager at the quarry who passed away at the age of 35.

**Read more: “**[**How Crocodiles Survived the Asteroid That Killed the Dinosaurs**](https://nautil.us/how-crocodiles-survived-the-asteroid-that-killed-the-dinosaurs-1286003)**”**

Proudlove’s dinosaur namesake is one of several iguanodontians identified in southern England over the past few years after a detailed analysis of one of two major groups (mantellisaurus) was [published](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02693445.2023.2234156) in 2023. Like its iguanodon relatives, the newly described dinosaur had characteristic thumbspikes and ate only plants. According to the team, the over 16-foot-long dinosaur weighed in at around 3,300-4,400 pounds, and its bones were still forming, indicating it may have been a juvenile. An adult might have been twice as big as the rhino-sized specimen unearthed, the team says.

Its genus name comes from the Latin for swamp as a nod to the marsh-like environment that covered England around 125 million years ago during the Cretaceous period. And while _P. proudlovii_ dined on wetland plants, there were other dinosaurs dining on it. According to the team, the remains of a _Baryonyx walkeri_, a type of spinosaur, was unearthed from the same quarry harboring a grim surprise.

“_Paludohadros_ was found just 100 meters away from _Baryonyx_, whose fossils we also look after at the Natural History Museum,” study author Susannah Maidment of the Natural History Museum, London said in a statement. “While Baryonyx is best known for eating fish, this dinosaur’s last meal also included a baby iguanodontian.”

It’s unclear what species the spinosaur’s dinner belonged to, but it’s safe to say _P. proudlovii_ may have munched while glancing over its shoulder.

Finally, if you’re wondering what discoveries await in the rest of the museum’s collections, help is on the way. “I’m now going to go through the Natural History Museum’s iguanodontian collections to identify what’s there as part of my PhD,” study author Ricardo Sacamoto said. “This could lead to the discovery of more new dinosaur species that haven’t yet been recognized.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Inside the Mind of a Narcissist
content:
In recent years, the term “narcissist” has been swung around like a sword in the dark. In everyday use, it came to describe anyone guilty of routine selfishness. The word is lay shorthand for a clinical diagnosis, narcissistic personality disorder, defined by grandiosity, extreme need for admiration, and difficulty with empathy. But milder versions of these traits, such as self-confidence and ambition, can be adaptive, and plenty of successful, well-functioning adults have employed them to get ahead.

There is a lot we still don’t know about how people with narcissistic traits relate to others and to themselves. Or how these traits show up in the workings of the brain. Recently, a team of scientists from Finland set out to get a better handle on what narcissism may look like in the brain during the kinds of socially complex interactions one might encounter in daily life. They called their work the “Faces of Narcissism” project.

**Read more: “**[**What Makes a Narcissist?**](https://nautil.us/what-makes-a-narcissist-493405)**”**

From an online survey of 1,000 people, the researchers chose 58 people to participate in brain scans. This group included people who scored on the high ends and the low ends in confidence, entitlement, and attention seeking, traits associated with narcissism of the grandiose type. None of the individuals selected had been diagnosed with the clinical disorder.

Studies of empathy often rely on simple tests of how a person responds to a picture of a sad face, or an image or video of someone in pain, for example a person responding to a needle prick. But the human social world is much more tangled than that, so the scientists presented their subjects with videos of different social scenarios requiring some form of evaluation and interpretation from the viewer. While inside a scanner that traced the flow of blood through their brains, all of the subjects watched videos of an actor telling personal stories, recounting times they were admired or episodes where they were snubbed. Then someone gave the actor feedback that was meant to sting, suggesting either that the admiration was undeserved or that the rejection was the actor’s own fault.

The team found that the brains of people low in narcissistic traits moved in sync, with neural activity in areas related to interpreting social situations and to cognitive empathy following a similar pattern. The brains of those high in narcissistic traits were less in sync, suggesting they did not share the actor’s feelings of embarrassment. The scientists published their [results](https://doi.org/10.1093/cercor/bhag175) in the journal _Cerebral Cortex_.

“People with a high number of narcissistic traits respond to another person’s vulnerable experience differently than others,” said study author Matias Piispanen, a researcher at Aalto University in Espoo, in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1148543). “They may attune to interaction in a different way, pay attention to different aspects of it, or make different interpretations of what is happening.”

The brains of those high in narcissistic traits weren’t silent, they were just inconsistent with one another. The scientists suggested this means that these individuals might be paying attention to different details or reading the situation differently, rather than not caring at all. The findings tie back to earlier [work](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00332747.1955.11023008) by sociologist Erving Goffman, who argued in the 1950s that humans tend to work together to protect one another’s public image. Goffman called this “facework.” The Finnish research team proposed that people high in narcissistic traits may do this kind of work differently, which could partly explain why their interactions may sometimes feel less genuine.

The scientists wanted to test the intuitive responses of their subjects, so they did not give them any hints about what to feel. “Participants were not specifically instructed to empathize with the narrator’s experience,” noted Piispanen. “This allowed us to observe how they spontaneously tracked and processed a complex social situation as it played out.”

If the research holds up, it suggests that “saving face” may have a neural signature, and that people high in narcissistic traits show less of it. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Why Your Boss Might Live Longer Than You
content:
Being an entrepreneur is a high-risk, high-reward endeavor, but a new [study](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0883902626000856) suggests one of those rewards may be a longer life.

A team of economic researchers from the Stevens Institute of Technology uncovered the potential link using data from the Health and Retirement Study. This longitudinal study monitors the health of Americans aged 50 and older, along with related lifestyle factors like employment. In this investigation, the team relied on data from more than 27,000 people recorded from a period between 1998 and 2020.

**Read more: “**[**Is This the First Corporate Psychopath?**](https://nautil.us/is-this-the-first-corporate-psychopath-1286033)**”**

Surprisingly, they found that those who reported their jobs as “self-employed” had a 10 percent reduced risk of mortality during the study period (compared to those who worked for a wage). Additionally, the longer someone was self-employed, the greater the mortality benefits they saw.

It’s a bit counterintuitive. After all, entrepreneurship tends to be associated with stress—a notorious killer. So why might bosses live longer than employees?

The secret could be self-reliance and a sense of purpose. (A previous [study](http://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0022399913000391) found that those with a greater sense of purpose in life showed a reduced risk of stroke.)

“Most people think of entrepreneurship as extremely stressful, and it certainly can be,” Cristiano Bellavitis, associate professor in the School of Business at Stevens Institute of Technology, explained in a [statement](https://www.stevens.edu/news/stevens-study-points-to-the-longevity-advantage-of-entrepreneurship). “But entrepreneurship also gives people a high degree of autonomy and the opportunity to pursue something they genuinely love or care about. Our findings suggest those benefits may have lasting effects.”

In fact, the apparent benefits of entrepreneurship were mediated by mental health. According to the team, self-employed individuals tended to score better on measures like loneliness and depression, two psychological factors linked to reduced longevity. However, these mental health benefits only explained 3.7 percent of the mortality benefit.

In a much less counterintuitive finding, the team discovered that opportunity-driven entrepreneurs—those who ventured on their own because they wanted to—got the bulk of the benefits. Necessity-driven entrepreneurs, who likely self-started after a job loss or labor market restructuring, didn’t see the same increase in longevity. According to the team, this wrinkle fits with a sense of individual agency driving the mortality benefits.

“What seems to matter is not entrepreneurship alone, but the circumstances under which people enter it,” Bellavitis said. “When entrepreneurship reflects greater choice and opportunity, the autonomy and sense of purpose that can come with it may provide psychological benefits that extend beyond financial rewards.”

Of course, there are plenty of caveats. Because this is an observational study, the researchers can’t say for sure which way the arrow of causation points. It’s entirely possible that healthier individuals are also more likely to start their own businesses. The team tried to investigate this possibility using data from a study on monozygotic twins, and they found a similar pattern (reduced mortality for entrepreneurs partially mediated by mental health), but stressed that it only examines genetic and early life effects, not health per se.

Additionally, the Health Retirement Study doesn’t include data on what kinds of enterprises these entrepreneurs are engaged in (or how successful they were). While they did control for income, the study treats a S&P 500-beating day-trader the same as a failed restaurateur.

But the main takeaway, according to the team, is that independence and purpose should be considered important longevity factors, regardless of whether you sign a paycheck or cash one. “Whether you’re an entrepreneur or an employee, finding ways to have ownership of your work and a reason to be excited about what you do every day is important for long-term well-being,” Bellavitis said. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: How We Control What Accents We Pick Up
content:
Accents are funny things. If you were raised in the south but moved to the north (like me), you may have lost even the residue of a Southern drawl (also me). But if you’re surrounded by twangy relatives during the holidays, you may find yourself sliding right back into it (again, me). Conversely, if you’ve got a nondescript accent and move somewhere with a strong regional dialect, you might pick that up, as well. Now a new [study](http://dx.doi.org/10.16995/labphon.24504) is shedding light on how our brains choose which features of accents to imitate.

Linguists from Ohio State University recruited 136 English-speaking Americans and played them a recording of a college-educated Australian woman pronouncing five words featuring different vowel sounds: bath, trap, kit, price, and near. Roughly a third of the participants were instructed to imitate the speaker’s Aussie accent, another third was explicitly told not to, and the final third was simply told to repeat the words. Afterwards, the participants completed a questionnaire asking them their views of the mystery Australian and what they noticed about how she pronounced the words.

**Read more: “**[**The Key to Multilingualism Lies in the Ears, Not the Mouth**](https://nautil.us/the-key-to-multilingualism-lies-in-the-ears-not-the-mouth-1285745)**”**

Acoustic analysis revealed the participants were adept at both imitating the foreign accent or refraining, depending on instructions. But things got really interesting with the group that was merely told to repeat the speaker. When left to their own devices, these participants tended to only mimic a few features of the accent, like dropping the “r” in “near” to pronounce it “nee-uh.” Follow-up questionnaires revealed these features tended to be the ones that drew the people’s attention.

“People are pretty good at controlling whether they sound like somebody, if you ask them to, but accent features that they find socially meaningful and notable will interfere with that,” study author Kathryn Campbell-Kibler explained in a [statement](https://news.osu.edu/how-much-control-do-we-have-over-picking-up-an-accent-a-lot-study-finds/). “Basically, if we don’t tell you whether or not to imitate somebody, you’re going to sound like them on the bits that you notice or think are interesting.”

The team also uncovered some tension between what the participants expected to hear and what they actually heard. For example, participants copying the Australian vowels in words like “trap,” tended to overdo it, but pulled back when they heard the speaker use a broader vowel sound in words like the one in “bath.”

Finally, the researchers also noted that there was no hesitation among the group instructed to imitate the Aussie accent. According to the team, the enthusiasm was likely due to English speakers’ esteem for Australians. “The model talker spoke a dialect that was likely to be in high regard for the participants, allowing us to examine the imitation of different dialect features in a prestigious variety,” the researchers wrote. “You don’t feel like you’re making fun of somebody in the same way that you might if it was a stigmatized group,” Campbell-Kibler added.

It also may explain why _Crocodile Dundee_ got two sequels. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Marcus Aurelius on the Good Luck of Your Bad Luck
content:
[![Image 1: Marcus Aurelius on the Good Luck of Your Bad Luck](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/meditations_robinwaterfield.jpg?fit=320%2C496&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Meditations-Annotated-Marcus-Aurelius/dp/1541673859/?tag=braipick-20)

Most people live with a great deal more suffering than is visible to even the most proximate and sensitive onlooker. Many have survived things both unimaginable and invisible to the outside world. This has been the case since the dawn of our species, for human nature has hardly changed beneath the continually repainted façade of our social sanctions — human beings have always been capable of inflicting tremendous pain on each other and capable of triumphal healing.

There is, however, a peculiar modern phenomenon that might best be described as a culture of competitive trauma. In recent times, the touching human longing for sympathy, that impulse to have our suffering recognized and validated, has grown distorted by a troubling compulsion for broadcast-suffering and comparative validity. Personhoods are staked on the cards dealt and not the hands played, as if we evolved the opposable thumbs of our agency for nothing. In memoirs and reality shows, across infinite Alexandrian scrolls of social media feeds, the unlucky events of life have become the currency of attention and identification.

[![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/artyoung_treesatnight7.jpg?resize=680%2C1070&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/last-appeal-from-trees-at-night-by-art-young_print?curator=brainpicker)

Drawing by Art Young from [_Trees at Night_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/08/06/trees-at-night-art-young/), 1926. (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/last-appeal-from-trees-at-night-by-art-young_print?curator=brainpicker).)

There is a way, with moderate moral imagination and considerable countercultural courage, to subvert this tendency without turning away from the reality and magnitude of suffering that we do live with — a way to esteem in attention and admiration not the unluckiness of what has happened to us but the luckiness that, despite it, we have become the people we are and have the lives we have by the sheer unwillingness to stay in that small dark place, which is at heart a willingness to be larger than our hurt selves.

It is not a new way of reframing personal narrative (which, after all, is [the neuropsychological pillar of identity](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/01/15/oliver-sacks-identity-self-narrative/)). It is a very old way, common to many of the world’s [ancient traditions](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/11/06/alan-watts-swimming-headless/) but most clearly and creatively articulated by the Stoic philosopher **Marcus Aurelius** (April 26, 121–March 17, 180).

[![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/10/marcusaurelius.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Meditations-Annotated-Marcus-Aurelius/dp/1541673859/?tag=braipick-20)

Marcus Aurelius

Because the modern mind calculates validity of vantage point by estimating the comparative value of suffering, it must be observed that, later in life, Marcus Aurelius had it easier than most of his contemporaries, being Emperor; it must also be observed that, earlier in life, he had it harder than most, being a [fatherless child](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/10/07/marcus-aurelius-meditations-father/) and a [queer teenager](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/02/16/marcus-aurelius-in-love-amy-richlin/) in Roman antiquity, epochs before the notion of LGBTQ rights, or for that matter most human rights. It is hardly surprising that he turned to Stoicism for succor and training in living with the uncertainty of events and the certainty of loss.

His timeless [**_Meditations_**](https://www.amazon.com/Meditations-Annotated-Marcus-Aurelius/dp/1541673859/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://www.worldcat.org/title/meditations/oclc/1200832206&referer=brief_results)), newly translated and annotated by the British classics scholar Robin Waterfield, were the original self-help — Marcus wrote these notebooks primarily as notes to himself while learning how to live: how to live with more agency, equanimity, and even joy in a world violently unpredictable at all times and especially so in his time.

[![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/greatwave_hokusai.jpg?resize=680%2C457&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/the-great-wave-off-kanagawa-by-hokusai-1831_print?curator=brainpicker)

_The Great Wave off Kanagawa_ by Japanese artist Hokusai, 1831. (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/the-great-wave-off-kanagawa-by-hokusai-1831_print?curator=brainpicker) and [as a face mask](https://society6.com/brainpicker/collection/vintage-science-face-masks?curator=brainpicker), benefitting The Nature Conservancy.)

In one of those self-counsels, Marcus Aurelius considers the key to regarding one’s own life, and living it, with positive realism:

> Be like a headland: the waves beat against it continuously, but it stands fast and around it the boiling water dies down. “It’s my rotten luck that this has happened to me.” On the contrary, “It’s my good luck that, although this has happened to me, I still feel no distress, since I’m unbruised by the present and unconcerned about the future.” What happened could have happened to anyone, but not everyone could have carried on without letting it distress him. So why regard the incident as a piece of bad luck rather than seeing your avoidance of distress as a piece of good luck? Do you generally describe a person as unlucky when his nature worked well? Or do you count it as a malfunction of a person’s nature when it succeeds in securing the outcome it wanted?

[![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/hasuikawase1.jpg?resize=680%2C1014&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/spring-moon-at-ninomiya-beach-by-hasui-kawase-1931_print?sku=s6-19564891p4a1v46?curator=brainpicker)

_Spring Moon at Ninomiya Beach_, 1931 — one of Hasui Kawase’s [vintage Japanese woodblocks](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/03/22/hasui-kawase-prints/). (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/spring-moon-at-ninomiya-beach-by-hasui-kawase-1931_print?sku=s6-19564891p4a1v46?curator=brainpicker).)

With an eye to “what human nature wants” — what life ultimately demands as it lives itself through us, and what our highest answer is — he concludes:

> Can what happened to you stop you from being fair, high-minded, moderate, conscientious, unhasty, honest, moral, self-reliant, and so on — from possessing all the qualities that, when present, enable a man’s[*](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/10/17/ursula-k-le-guin-gender/) nature to be fulfilled? So then, whenever something happens that might cause you distress, remember to rely on this principle: this is not bad luck, but bearing it valiantly is good luck.

Complement with an equally counterintuitive and perspective-broadening modern case for [the luckiness of death](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/07/25/richard-dawkins-death/) and Alan Watts on [the ambiguity of good and bad luck](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/11/06/alan-watts-swimming-headless/), then revisit other highlights from the indispensable [**_Meditations_**](https://www.amazon.com/Meditations-Annotated-Marcus-Aurelius/dp/1541673859/?tag=braipick-20): Marcus Aurelius on [how to handle disappointing people](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/04/13/marcus-aurelius-meditations-robin-waterfield/), [the key to living with presence](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/05/20/marcus-aurelius-meditations-mortality-presence/), [the most potent motivation for work](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/01/03/marcus-aurelius-meditations-bed-work/), and [how to begin each day for maximum serenity of mind](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/01/03/marcus-aurelius-meditations-bed-work/).
